chunk.chapter_title: 65. The palace is filled with the sound of distress
chunk.text:
CHAPTER 65 
The palace is filled with the sound of distress 
THE night having passed, at dawn, according to custom, the 
bards arrived at the palace of the king, the traditional singers, 
those versed in rhetoric and in the history of the dynasty, and 
skilled musicians acquainted with rhythm and melody, began to 
sing the praises of the king. The sound of their eulogies and 
their songs filled the whole palace. Others uttering tributes 
and clapping their bands recited the monarch's wonderful deeds. 
The birds in the trees near the palace and those confined in 
cages awoke and sang. Their notes mingled with the salutations 
of the brahmins, the music of the vinas, the chanting of the holy 
names of God and the praises of those describing the great deeds 
of the king. Eunuchs and servants stood near, ready to serve, 
as was their wont. Those who attended to the ablutions of 
the king, brought water scented with fragrant perfumes, in 
pitchers of gold. Charming and well-attired men and women 
came with oil, unguents, mirrors, combs, towels and other 
articles and all that was needed by the king was provided 
according to custom. Till sunrise, all awaited the king, then 
they addressed each other saying : " How is this, has his majesty 
not yet risen ? " Then the women, other than Kaushalya, who 
formerly attended on the king, began to waken their lord as was 
their usage. 
Having with affecrion and skill touched the body 
of the monarch, they found no sign of life in him. Then the 
women, knowing well the motion of the pulse and understanding 
the signs of sleep, began to tremble perceiving the king's 
condition. Fearing that the king no longer breathed, they shook 
like the narcai• grass in the midst of a flowing stream, and slowly 
became aware that their sovereign had passed away. 
The Queens, Kaushalya and Sumitra, overcome with grief 
on account of the depanurc of their sons, lay as if dead. Sutfering 
had rendered the chief queen pale and her body feeble. The 
two queens, their splendour dimmed by sorrow, resembled the 
stars hidden by clouds.

brief.summary_1line: Palace attendants arrive to awaken the king with music and ritual, only to discover he has died, plunging the palace into grief.

image_candidates.scene_text: At dawn musicians and bards fill the palace halls with song while servants wait with golden pitchers of scented water for the king to awaken.
Attendant women gently touch the king's body and recoil in terror as they realize he no longer breathes.
Queen Kaushalya and Sumitra lie pale and motionless in grief, like dim stars hidden behind dark clouds.

deep.rich_summary: At dawn the royal palace follows its daily ritual: bards, musicians, brahmins, and attendants gather to awaken the king with praises, music, and ceremony. Servants prepare perfumes, oils, and golden vessels for the king’s morning ablutions while the entire court waits for him to rise. When he does not appear, the women of the palace attempt to wake him. Touching his body, they realize with growing dread that he shows no sign of life. Their fear turns to certainty: the king has died during the night. The palace, once filled with praise and music, becomes a place of shock and grief. Queen Kaushalya and Queen Sumitra, already broken by the exile of their sons, lie overwhelmed by sorrow, their faded splendor compared to stars hidden behind clouds. The scene marks the tragic consequence of Rama’s exile and the collapse of royal order in Ayodhya.

highlight_spans.why: The chapter title frames the entire episode as one of palace-wide grief and foreshadows the tragic discovery.
The pivotal moment when attendants realize the king is dead, turning the ceremonial morning into tragedy.
The vivid simile of women trembling like grass in a stream conveys their shock and fear as they understand the king has died.
The poetic comparison of the grieving queens to stars hidden by clouds underscores the dimming of royal glory and hope.

top_scenes.scene_text: At dawn the palace courtyard fills with bards, brahmins, musicians, birds, and attendants singing and playing instruments while the golden palace awaits the king’s awakening.
Royal attendants gently try to awaken the king in his chamber, then recoil in shock as they realize his body is lifeless.
Queen Kaushalya and Queen Sumitra lie pale and grief-stricken in the dim palace chamber, their sorrow likened to stars hidden behind dark clouds.
